name: surface air relative humidity
title: Surface Air Relative Humidity
abstract: Surface air relative humidity is the ratio of actual water vapour pressure to saturation vapour pressure at the same temperature and pressure. Dimensionless and bounded [0, 1], it quantifies how close the air is to saturation, controlling evapotranspiration rates, dew and frost formation, and human thermal comfort.

name: surface air temperature
title: Surface Air Temperature
abstract: Surface air temperature is the temperature of the atmosphere measured at standard screen height (1.5–2 m above ground) inside a radiation-shielded ventilated enclosure. It is the most fundamental climate variable, driving saturation vapour pressure, snowmelt, crop phenology, and energy balance calculations worldwide.

name: standard surface air temperature
title: Standard Surface Air Temperature
abstract: Standard surface air temperature is surface air temperature expressed in Kelvin, the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature. It is physically identical to surface air temperature but uses the absolute scale required by equations where temperature appears as a physical quantity rather than a relative difference.

name: dew point temperature
title: Dew Point Temperature
abstract: Dew point temperature is the temperature to which air must be cooled at constant pressure and water vapour content for condensation to begin. It is a direct measure of absolute humidity — unlike relative humidity it does not change with temperature — and is used to calculate actual vapour pressure, relative humidity, and vapour pressure deficit.

name: land surface temperature
title: Land Surface Temperature
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) is the radiometric skin temperature of the land surface, retrieved from thermal infrared satellite observations after correcting for surface emissivity. It represents the surface temperature rather than the overlying air temperature and is the key variable controlling surface energy partitioning, urban heat islands, and remote-sensing drought indices.

name: scalar wind speed
title: Scalar Wind Speed
abstract: Scalar wind speed is the magnitude of the horizontal wind velocity vector, measured at standard height of 10 m above ground. It is the primary wind variable in meteorological and hydrological applications — entering the Penman-Monteith evapotranspiration formula, wind energy assessment, and dust and wave generation models — and carries no directional information.

name: scalar wind gust speed
title: Scalar Wind Gust Speed
abstract: Scalar wind gust speed is the maximum instantaneous wind speed recorded within a defined sampling interval, conventionally the highest 3-second average within each 10-minute observation period. It characterises short-duration intensity peaks relevant for structural loading, aviation safety, fire weather, and extreme event analysis.

name: wind speed direction
title: Wind Speed Direction
abstract: Wind speed direction is the compass bearing from which wind originates, measured in degrees clockwise from true north. It is the angular component of the wind vector — combined with scalar wind speed it fully defines horizontal wind. Standard meteorological convention reports the direction the wind comes FROM, opposite to oceanographic convention.

name: surface atmospheric pressure
title: Surface Atmospheric Pressure
abstract: Surface atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air column above a unit area at the station elevation. It varies with altitude, weather systems, and temperature. In climatological applications it enters the psychrometric constant for evapotranspiration calculations and the altitude correction of temperature observations.

name: sunshine duration
title: Sunshine Duration
abstract: Sunshine duration is the number of hours per day during which direct solar irradiance exceeds 120 W/m², as defined by WMO. It is the most widely available proxy for cloudiness at historical climate stations and is used to estimate daily global solar radiation via the Ångström-Prescott empirical formula when direct radiation measurements are unavailable.

name: piché evaporation
title: Piché Evaporation
abstract: Piché evaporation is the water loss measured by a Piché evaporimeter — an inverted graduated glass tube with a wetted filter paper disc exposed to ambient air. It integrates the combined effect of temperature, humidity, and wind speed on atmospheric evaporative demand, and has been widely recorded at climatological stations as a proxy for pan evaporation before automatic sensors became standard.

name: solar radiation
title: Solar Radiation
abstract: Solar radiation is the total solar energy received per unit area over a given time period — the cumulative integral of solar irradiance over the timestep. It is the primary energy input to the land surface, driving evapotranspiration, photosynthesis, and the surface energy balance, and is expressed in kJ/m² or MJ/m² per day in agricultural and hydrological applications.

name: solar irradiance
title: Solar Irradiance
abstract: Solar irradiance is the instantaneous solar power flux received per unit area of a horizontal surface, expressed in W/m². It is the rate form of solar radiation — the instantaneous input that, integrated over a timestep, gives cumulative solar radiation in J/m² or MJ/m². It is the standard variable in photovoltaic energy assessment and the direct input to energy balance calculations.

name: precipitation
title: Water Precipitation
abstract: Precipitation is all atmospheric water reaching the land surface — rain, snow, hail, sleet, and freezing rain — measured as accumulated water depth per unit time. It is the primary input to the terrestrial water cycle and the fundamental driver of streamflow, groundwater recharge, soil moisture, and drought.

name: rainfall
title: Rain of Liquid Water
abstract: Rainfall is liquid precipitation reaching the ground surface, measured as accumulated water depth per unit time at a point. It is the primary atmospheric input to the terrestrial water cycle and the main driver of surface runoff, soil moisture recharge, and streamflow generation in non-glacial catchments.

name: water level
title: Water Level
abstract: Water level, or stage height, is the elevation of the water surface at a gauging station relative to a fixed local datum. It is the primary continuous hydrometric observation, measured with pressure transducers, float gauges, or ultrasonic sensors, and converted to discharge via a site-specific stage-discharge rating curve.

name: rating curve coefficient
title: Rating Curve Coefficient
abstract: The rating curve coefficient is the scale parameter of the power-law stage-discharge relationship Q = a(h − h₀)^b. It controls the magnitude of discharge at a given stage above the zero-flow level and is calibrated site-specifically from concurrent stage and discharge measurements. Its units depend on the exponent b, making direct cross-site comparison dimensionally inconsistent.

name: rating curve exponent
title: Rating Curve Exponent
abstract: The rating curve exponent is the shape parameter of the power-law stage-discharge relationship Q = a(h − h₀)^b. It controls how steeply discharge increases with stage and is dimensionless. For natural river channels the exponent typically falls between 1.5 and 2.5; the theoretical value for a wide rectangular channel under Manning's equation is 5/3 ≈ 1.67.

name: zero-flow stage
title: Zero-Flow Stage
abstract: The zero-flow stage is the gauge height at which discharge is theoretically zero in the power-law rating curve Q = a(h − h₀)^b. It defines the effective datum of the rating relationship and corresponds physically to the elevation of the hydraulic control that governs stage at the gauge — typically the crest of a natural riffle, a bedrock sill, or a weir.
synonyms: Gauge Datum | Stage Offset | Effective Zero

name: streamflow
title: Streamflow
abstract: Streamflow is the volumetric rate of water flowing past a cross-section of a watercourse. It is the primary output variable of the terrestrial water cycle, integrating the contributions of direct runoff, subsurface lateral flow, and baseflow from the entire upstream drainage basin.

name: standard streamflow
title: Standard Streamflow
abstract: Standard streamflow is river discharge expressed in the SI unit of m³/s — the conventional reporting standard for hydrological databases, models, and design calculations. It is equivalent to streamflow but fixes the time unit to seconds, as opposed to unit-converted variants such as specific streamflow (mm/day) or annual volume (Mm³/year).

name: drainage area
title: Drainage Area
abstract: Drainage area is the total land surface that contributes surface runoff to a defined stream cross-section, bounded by the topographic watershed divide. It is the primary scaling variable in hydrology — setting the magnitude of catchment response to precipitation — and a static structural property of the basin that does not change with weather or season.
synonyms: Basin Area | Catchment Area | Upstream Area

name: specific streamflow
title: Specific Streamflow
abstract: Specific streamflow is streamflow normalised by drainage area, expressing volumetric discharge as a water depth per unit time — the same dimensions as rainfall. Normalisation removes the effect of basin size, allowing direct comparison of runoff response across catchments of different areas and direct plotting against precipitation.

name: blue reflectance
title: Blue Reflectance
abstract: Blue reflectance is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface in the blue portion of the visible spectrum (~450–520 nm). Chlorophyll absorbs strongly here, making healthy vegetation show low blue reflectance. The blue band is highly susceptible to atmospheric scattering, and is used in the Enhanced Vegetation Index specifically to correct for aerosol effects.

name: green reflectance
title: Green Reflectance
abstract: Green reflectance is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface in the green portion of the visible spectrum (~525–600 nm). Vegetation shows a local reflectance peak here — the green peak — because chlorophyll absorption is weaker than in the adjacent red and blue bands. Open water reflects green relatively well compared to NIR, which is the physical basis of water body indices.

name: red reflectance
title: Red Reflectance
abstract: Red reflectance is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface in the red portion of the visible spectrum (~620–700 nm), where chlorophyll a and b absorb strongly for photosynthesis. Healthy dense vegetation shows very low red reflectance; bare soil and impervious surfaces show higher values.

name: near-infrared reflectance
title: Near-Infrared Reflectance
abstract: Near-infrared reflectance is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface in the near-infrared portion of the spectrum (~700–900 nm), where there is no chlorophyll absorption but strong scattering by leaf cell structure. Healthy vegetation shows very high NIR reflectance; open water shows near-zero values. This contrast with the red and green bands underpins virtually all vegetation and water body indices.

name: red-edge reflectance
title: Red-Edge Reflectance
abstract: Red-edge reflectance is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface in the narrow spectral transition zone between chlorophyll absorption and the NIR plateau (~700–740 nm). Because chlorophyll absorption is partial rather than total in this region, red-edge reflectance remains sensitive to chlorophyll concentration even in dense canopies where the red band is already driven to near-zero, making it the preferred band for quantitative chlorophyll estimation.

name: shortwave infrared reflectance
title: Shortwave Infrared Reflectance
abstract: Shortwave infrared reflectance is the fraction of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface in the shortwave infrared portion of the spectrum (~1400–2500 nm). Liquid water absorbs strongly in this region, making it sensitive to vegetation canopy water content and open water detection. Built-up surfaces show relatively high SWIR reflectance, a property exploited in the MNDWI to suppress urban false positives in water mapping.

name: thermal infrared brightness temperature
title: Thermal Infrared Brightness Temperature
abstract: Thermal infrared brightness temperature is the equivalent blackbody temperature derived from emitted thermal radiance measured in the long-wave infrared atmospheric window (~8–14 μm). Unlike reflective bands, it registers emitted surface radiation rather than reflected solar radiation. It is the primary input for land surface temperature retrieval and for thermal-based drought indicators such as the Temperature Condition Index.

name: x-band radar backscatter
title: X-Band Radar Backscatter
abstract: X-band radar backscatter is the SAR backscatter coefficient measured at ~8–12 GHz frequency (~2.5–3.75 cm wavelength). The short wavelength produces fine spatial resolution and strong surface scattering, making X-band suited for high-resolution urban mapping, snow and ice monitoring, and detailed infrastructure assessment. Penetration into vegetation or soil is limited at this frequency.

name: c-band radar backscatter
title: C-Band Radar Backscatter
abstract: C-band radar backscatter is the SAR backscatter coefficient measured at ~4–8 GHz frequency (~3.75–7.5 cm wavelength). It is the most widely used SAR frequency in operational Earth observation, carried by Sentinel-1, ERS, RADARSAT, and RISAT. At this wavelength the signal interacts primarily with vegetation canopy surfaces and the upper soil layer, making C-band well suited for crop monitoring, flood mapping, sea ice classification, and open soil moisture retrieval.

name: l-band radar backscatter
title: L-Band Radar Backscatter
abstract: L-band radar backscatter is the SAR backscatter coefficient measured at ~1–2 GHz frequency (~15–30 cm wavelength). The wavelength is long enough to penetrate forest canopies and interact with large woody branches and trunks, while remaining sensitive to soil moisture beneath moderate vegetation cover. L-band is the primary band for forest biomass estimation and forest change detection at continental scale, operated by ALOS-2/PALSAR and the NISAR mission.

name: p-band radar backscatter
title: P-Band Radar Backscatter
abstract: P-band radar backscatter is the SAR backscatter coefficient measured at very low microwave frequencies (~0.3–1 GHz, ~30–100 cm wavelength). The long wavelength enables deep penetration through vegetation canopies and into the soil column, making P-band uniquely suited for forest above-ground biomass estimation and sub-canopy structure characterisation. It is the primary band of the upcoming ESA BIOMASS mission.

name: simple ratio vegetation index
title: Simple Ratio Vegetation Index
abstract: The Simple Ratio (SR) is the earliest quantitative vegetation index, proposed by Carl Jordan in 1969 as a means to estimate leaf area index from the ratio of near-infrared to red light measured on the forest floor. It established the foundational principle — that the contrast between NIR and red reflectance encodes information about vegetation — that underlies every subsequent index in the field.

name: normalized difference vegetation index
title: Normalized Difference Vegetation Index
abstract: The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) is the most widely used vegetation index in remote sensing, proposed by Rouse and colleagues in 1973 using early Landsat data. It quantifies vegetation presence and density by normalizing the contrast between near-infrared and red reflectance into a bounded −1 to +1 scale, making values comparable across scenes, dates, and sensors. Despite known limitations in dense canopies and over sparse cover, NDVI remains the standard baseline index for vegetation monitoring across virtually every satellite platform.

name: soil-adjusted vegetation index
title: Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index
abstract: The Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index (SAVI) was proposed by Alfredo Huete in 1988 to address a specific limitation of NDVI in landscapes where bare soil is partially visible within a pixel. By introducing a soil adjustment factor L into the denominator, SAVI suppresses the influence of soil background reflectance on the vegetation signal, producing more reliable estimates of vegetation cover in semi-arid, dryland, and early-season agricultural contexts.

name: modified soil-adjusted vegetation index
title: Modified Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index
abstract: The Modified Soil-Adjusted Vegetation Index (MSAVI) was proposed by Qi and colleagues in 1994 as an improvement over SAVI, replacing the fixed soil adjustment factor L with a self-adjusting term computed directly from the NIR and red reflectance values of each pixel. This eliminates the need for a user-supplied parameter and produces a more consistently optimal soil correction across the full range of vegetation cover densities, from bare soil to closed canopy.

name: enhanced vegetation index
title: Enhanced Vegetation Index
abstract: The Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI) was developed by Huete and colleagues for the MODIS sensor and validated in 2002, addressing two limitations of NDVI simultaneously: saturation in dense tropical canopies and sensitivity to atmospheric aerosols. By incorporating a blue band term for aerosol correction alongside background adjustment coefficients, EVI maintains sensitivity in high-biomass environments where NDVI plateaus. It is a standard NASA data product distributed globally from the Terra and Aqua MODIS instruments.

name: red-edge normalized difference vegetation index
title: Red-Edge Normalized Difference Vegetation Index
abstract: The Red-Edge Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDRE) was proposed by Gitelson and Merzlyak in 1994 as a variant of NDVI that substitutes a narrow red-edge band for the broad red band. By operating in the spectral transition zone between chlorophyll absorption and NIR scattering (~700–740 nm), NDRE is substantially more sensitive to chlorophyll concentration and less prone to saturation in dense canopies than conventional NDVI. Operationally relevant only since the launch of Sentinel-2 in 2015, which provided the first widely accessible satellite red-edge bands at useful spatial resolution.

name: chlorophyll index red-edge
title: Chlorophyll Index red-edge
abstract: The Chlorophyll Index red-edge (CIre) was formalized by Gitelson and colleagues in 2003 as a ratio-form index designed to estimate leaf chlorophyll content more directly than NDRE. By expressing the relationship between NIR and red-edge reflectance as a simple ratio minus one, CIre maintains a near-linear relationship with chlorophyll concentration across a wider range of canopy types and species than normalized difference indices. Like NDRE, it requires a red-edge band and has become operationally relevant primarily through Sentinel-2.

name: normalized difference water vegetation index
title: Normalized Difference Water Vegetation Index
abstract: The Normalized Difference Water Vegetation Index (NDWI-V), proposed by Gao (1996), estimates vegetation canopy liquid water content from satellite imagery by contrasting near-infrared and shortwave-infrared reflectance. Because liquid water absorbs strongly in the SWIR while leaf cell structure scatters NIR efficiently, healthy well-watered vegetation yields high NIR and suppressed SWIR, producing positive values that decline as canopy water stress increases.

name: vegetation health index
title: Vegetation Health Index
abstract: The Vegetation Health Index (VHI) is a satellite-derived drought indicator that combines a vegetation-greenness signal with a thermal-stress signal into a single composite score, without requiring ground-based meteorological data. It is computed as a weighted average of the Vegetation Condition Index (VCI), derived from NDVI, and the Temperature Condition Index (TCI), derived from land surface or brightness temperature, each normalised against its own historical range at a given location. Developed by Felix Kogan between 1990 and 2001, VHI remains one of the most widely used remote sensing drought indices and underpins several national early-warning systems.

name: temperature condition index
title: Temperature Condition Index
abstract: The Temperature Condition Index (TCI) is a satellite-derived drought indicator that rescales brightness or land surface temperature against its own historical minimum and maximum at each location, in the same way the Vegetation Condition Index rescales NDVI. It captures thermal stress on vegetation as a complement to the moisture signal captured by VCI, and the two are combined into the composite Vegetation Health Index. It was introduced by Kogan (1995).

name: vegetation condition index
title: Vegetation Condition Index
abstract: The Vegetation Condition Index (VCI) is a satellite-derived drought indicator that rescales NDVI against its own historical minimum and maximum at each location, isolating the weather-driven component of vegetation greenness from persistent spatial differences due to soil type, ecosystem, or terrain. Introduced by Kogan (1990) and formalised by Liu and Kogan (1996), it is used both as a standalone drought indicator and as the moisture-related component of the composite Vegetation Health Index.

name: normalized difference water body index
title: Normalized Difference Water Body Index
abstract: The Normalized Difference Water Body Index (NDWI), proposed by McFeeters (1996), delineates open water bodies from multispectral imagery using the contrast between green and near-infrared reflectance. Open water shows high green and very low NIR reflectance, yielding positive values, while vegetation and bare soil produce negative values. It is the standard index for water body extraction and flood mapping.

name: normalized difference water body index modified
title: Normalized Difference Water Body Index Modified
abstract: The Modified Normalized Difference Water Body Index (MNDWI), proposed by Xu (2006), improves on McFeeters' NDWI for water extraction in urban and built-up environments by replacing the NIR band with shortwave-infrared. The substitution suppresses spurious water detections from built-up surfaces that contaminate NDWI results in urban scenes, while preserving the strong positive response of open water bodies.

name: standardized precipitation index
title: Standardized Precipitation Index
abstract: The Standardized Precipitation Index (SPI) is a multi-scalar meteorological drought index that fits a probability distribution to accumulated precipitation and converts it to a z-score on the standard normal scale. Its multi-scalar design — from one month to 24 months or more — allows it to characterise both short-term agricultural moisture stress and longer-term hydrological water deficit from a single statistical framework.

name: aggregate drought index
title: Aggregate Drought Index
abstract: Keyantash and Dracup's Aggregate Drought Index (ADI) is a PCA-based drought severity measure derived from six standardised hydrometeorological variables spanning precipitation, evapotranspiration, streamflow, reservoir storage, soil moisture, and snow water content. Unlike fixed-formula indices, ADI weights are specific to the historical dataset and region used to derive the principal components.

name: standardized streamflow index
title: Standardized Streamflow Index
abstract: The Standardized Streamflow Index (SSFI) applies the same statistical standardisation as SPI to monthly streamflow values, expressing streamflow anomalies on the standard normal scale. It is functionally equivalent to SRI for most practical purposes, having been developed independently with emphasis on the statistical properties and scaling behaviour of the resulting index.

name: standardized runoff index
title: Standardized Runoff Index
abstract: The Standardized Runoff Index (SRI) applies the same probability transform as SPI to accumulated streamflow or runoff, targeting hydrological drought directly rather than inferring it from an upstream meteorological deficit. It can be computed at multiple accumulation timescales, reflecting both short-term flow anomalies and longer-term aquifer or reservoir depletion.

name: standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index
title: Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index
abstract: The Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) extends the SPI methodology to the climatic water balance — precipitation minus reference evapotranspiration — rather than precipitation alone, typically fitted to a log-logistic distribution. Because it accounts for evaporative demand, SPEI responds to warming-driven drought intensification that pure precipitation indices miss.

name: composite drought index
title: Composite Drought Index
abstract: Waseem's Composite Drought Index (CDI) is a multivariate drought indicator that combines precipitation, streamflow, NDVI, and land surface temperature into a single entropy-weighted composite score. Weights are derived from each variable's historical variability via Shannon entropy, and the score is expressed as a weighted distance of current conditions from the historically driest state observed for that set of variables.

name: soil water deficit index
title: Soil Water Deficit Index
abstract: The Soil Water Deficit Index (SWDI) is an agricultural drought indicator that rescales observed soil moisture against the field capacity and wilting point of the soil, expressing remaining plant-available water as a dimensionless score. Positive or near-zero values indicate adequate or excess moisture; increasingly negative values indicate progressive depletion of plant-available water toward and below the wilting point.

name: evaporative stress index
title: Evaporative Stress Index
abstract: The Evaporative Stress Index (ESI) is a satellite-derived agricultural drought indicator that standardises the ratio of actual to reference evapotranspiration into a z-score. Anomalously low ratios indicate vegetation drawing less water than atmospheric demand would allow, signalling moisture limitation on transpiration. Because the ratio normalises by reference ET, ESI isolates the moisture-stress signal from seasonal variation in energy supply.
